stories.title: Study: Europe's record summer heat killed about 50,000 people in its cities, two-thirds of them because of climate change
paragraphs: Record heat across Europe this summer was linked to 50,391 deaths in 854 European cities between June and August, according to a study by researchers at Imperial College London reported by The Associated Press on Oct. 23, 2026. The study, due in an upcoming issue of Nature Health, found that 32,619 of those deaths, about 65 percent, happened because of the extra heat added by human-caused climate change, mostly from burning coal, oil and gas.

According to the AP, that toll is 71 percent higher than the previous deadliest summer the same researchers have tracked, 29,480 deaths in 2022. The authors told the AP the new figures are underestimates, because they leave out a deadly heat wave in May and cover only those 854 cities, which hold about 40 percent of Europe's population. About a third of the deaths came during an especially intense heat wave from June 17 to July 1, when temperatures ran 5.3 degrees Celsius (9.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal, co-author Garyfallos Konstantinoudis said. Italy, France, Spain and Germany had the highest death tolls, and more than half of those who died were 85 or older, though more than 800 people aged 20 to 44 also died.

The study's abstract says the team combined probabilistic climate attribution with city- and age-specific temperature and mortality relationships, comparing this summer with simulated conditions in a world without human-caused warming. The paper notes that Europe was about 2.5 degrees Celsius warmer in 2026 than in a preindustrial climate, and that the summer was confirmed as the hottest on record for western Europe. Lead author Clair Barnes told the AP that much of western and northern Europe's infrastructure "is just not designed to cope" with today's temperatures, and that the share of heat deaths attributable to warming has grown from about 45 percent in the early 2000s to 65 percent now.

The researchers checked their method against real-time government estimates, the AP reported: for Britain's May and June heat waves, the team calculated 2,700 excess deaths, while the U.K. health statistics agency counted 2,800. Outside experts quoted by the AP, including Howard Frumkin, former director of the U.S. National Center for Environmental Health, and Jonathan Patz of the University of Wisconsin-Madison, praised the methods and called for both better protection from heat and cuts in fossil fuel use.

stories.title: xAI launches the SpaceX Super Intelligence Partner Network, with more than 130 companies in early access
paragraphs: xAI announced the SpaceX Super Intelligence Partner Network on its x.ai news page on Oct. 22, 2026, describing it as its official program for companies building products, solutions and services with Grok for joint prospects and customers. According to the announcement on x.ai, the program gives partners access to training, tools and support for their work with those shared customers, and companies can apply at x.ai/partners.

The company says the network brings together two types of partners. Transformation Partners help customers deploy the Grok platform across the enterprise and create business value, while Marketplace Partners build the plugins and product integrations that let the Grok product suite work with the tools customers already use.

According to xAI, more than 130 companies took part in the program's early-access phase. The announcement says Transformation Partners are building capacity through a Forward Deployed Engineer accreditation program, with engineers trained at more than 30 organizations, and that Marketplace Partners are seeing growing adoption of their products alongside Grok. xAI says partners are already helping customers in every industry and around the world, from startups to Fortune 20 companies.

The announcement features launch partners including Bain, Snowflake, Booz Allen, MongoDB, Langfuse (part of ClickHouse), CodeRabbit, Endor Labs, NTT DATA, Sonar, Twilio and Zscaler, each represented by a named executive such as Snowflake's SVP of Engineering Vivek Raghunathan and MongoDB's Chief Product Officer Ben Cefalo.

stories.title: Anthropic hands its Agent Skills standard to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation
paragraphs: Anthropic said on Oct. 22 that it is donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). The AAIF sits under the Linux Foundation, and Anthropic says it co-founded the foundation with Block and OpenAI last year and had already donated its Model Context Protocol (MCP) to it. According to Anthropic, more than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since it published the standard in December 2025.

Anthropic describes a skill as a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. The company says it developed skills while working on Claude Code, which handled general knowledge work well but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. It says developers published thousands of skills on GitHub within weeks of the October 2025 launch, and that so far 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed.

As part of the donation, Anthropic says it is handing over the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization and the agentskills.io domain, and that people can keep using or contributing to the standard without joining the AAIF. Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and other companies will maintain it as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as lead maintainers. Anthropic says it has proposed a starting roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process and security guidance for people who write and install skills.

stories.title: At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA shows European banks, governments and robot makers building on open models
paragraphs: NVIDIA used its GTC Berlin event on Oct. 22, 2026 to publish a set of blog posts on how European organizations are building AI on open models running on infrastructure they control. In its financial-services post, NVIDIA says Revolut is rebuilding its technology stack on a single foundation model called PRAGMA, running on NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs and serving an initial 80 million customers. Revolut's head of AI, Pavel Nesterov, is quoted calling PRAGMA "the clearest proof yet" that a research breakthrough can become a production banking system.

The same post lists other banks and payment firms. According to NVIDIA, Lloyds Banking Group built a transaction foundation model called ATUM, neobank bunq's assistant Finn now runs on open-weight models at 60% of the cost per answer of leading closed models while matching their quality, Santander is an early adopter of NVIDIA's new Kumo family of open-weight models for structured financial data, and Stripe saw 42x faster data pipelines and 92% cost savings for its Radar fraud-detection platform in offline testing.

A second post covers the public sector. NVIDIA says Poland's eHealth Centre is building a medical-imaging platform to help physicians analyze X-rays, CT scans and MRI images, and that Poland's labor ministry, with Deloitte, is developing an agentic system meant to support more than 400 labor offices. The post also says secunet, NVIDIA, Red Hat and deepset are developing a sovereign cloud offering for classified information in German data centers, and that new synthetic-persona datasets for the U.K. and Germany, each with 1 million records, were released to test whether public-service models work consistently across communities.

In a third post, NVIDIA says it expanded its Cosmos platform for world models, which help physical AI systems such as robots and self-driving cars simulate the real world, with new training tools, Cosmos 3 Nano simulation models and Cosmos Data Factory blueprints. According to NVIDIA, Porsche expects the tools to cut repeated physical test drives by up to 90% across Volkswagen Group brands, and robot maker ANYbotics generated more than 1,500 synthetic video clips to train its industrial-inspection robots to spot liquid spills.

stories.title: OpenAI says thousands of AI agents analyzed a brain-cell gene atlas in 32 minutes and turned up new disease leads
paragraphs: OpenAI said on Oct. 21, 2026, that it worked with PerturbAI and Scripps Research to run thousands of AI agents, powered by its GPT-Rosalind model, over existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells. According to OpenAI, the analysis took 32 minutes, and the team estimated that comparable human analysis and literature review, done one gene disruption at a time, would take months to a year.

The data came from a whole-brain CRISPR atlas, which shows how disrupting individual genes affects different types of cells across the mouse brain. OpenAI says each agent investigated one gene disruption, analyzed the cells' responses, searched the scientific literature and proposed explanations, and the reports were combined into a 'reasoning atlas' linking genes, cellular effects, publications and possible mechanisms. OpenAI says the agents reproduced findings from human analyses, and that their judgments of novelty and scientific value matched those of blinded human experts.

Among the leads OpenAI describes: in the cerebellum, disrupting the gene Tsc2 changed the activity of dozens of genes involved in neuronal communication while disrupting its partner Tsc1 changed little, a difference OpenAI notes may be relevant to tuberous sclerosis. The agents also linked disruption of Dctn1, a gene whose mutations cause the Parkinson-like Perry syndrome, to higher activity of cholesterol-making genes, raising a question about cholesterol and neurodegeneration that human experts called novel and worth following up.

OpenAI also compared the approach with a single agent given the whole dataset using the same model and resources. At the largest workload, it says, the distributed agents cited more than 700 references versus 11 for the single agent, and blinded human experts preferred the distributed-agent reports 75% of the time. OpenAI says the reasoning atlas is available for researchers to explore and that the findings still need lab experiments to test the proposed mechanisms.

stories.title: Europe's Space Rider prototype crashes in a drop test after its main parafoil detaches
paragraphs: A full-scale test model of Space Rider, the European Space Agency's planned reusable spacecraft, crashed during an Oct. 6 drop test, Space.com reported on Oct. 22, 2026. According to ESA officials cited by Space.com, the vehicle's first drogue parachute deployed as planned, but its main steerable parafoil detached during deployment, leaving the prototype unable to slow down before it hit the ground.

An ESA spokesperson told Space.com that the test "was not completed as planned due to an anomaly during the parafoil deployment sequence" and that an independent investigation is underway to find the root cause. The minivan-sized mockup was released from a helicopter at about 2 miles (3 kilometers) over a military range on the Italian island of Sardinia, and ESA has since recovered all of its components, Space.com reports.

Space Rider is being built as Europe's first reusable orbital spacecraft: an uncrewed vehicle meant to carry experiments to orbit for up to two months and bring them back to Earth. According to Space.com, its wingless design relies on the parafoil to steer to a runway-style landing, and the drop test was meant to demonstrate that ability, which is key to reusing the vehicle.

Speaking at an ESA Council media briefing on Oct. 22, ESA's director of space transportation, Géraldine Naja, said the agency hopes the test will not force changes to the remaining schedule, adding that the remaining qualification activities "are not on the critical path" of Space Rider's development. Space.com notes this was the first drop test since a May attempt that was called off before release.
